results.title: SF Compute raises $40m for AI compute marketplace offering - DCD
results.author: Georgia Butler
highlights:
Series A funding will be used to expand marketplace offering

December 02, 2025

By
: Georgia Butler 

SF Compute has secured $40 million in a Series A equity financing round for the expansion of its AI compute marketplace.

The San Francisco-based startup was valued at $300 million in the funding round, reports the Wall Street Journal.

 

 – SF Compute 

SF Compute's marketplace enables buyers of GPU capacity to resell their unused capacity. The company says this can help combat the risk of overbuilding data center capacity and help customers that are looking to access GPUs on a flexible basis to avoid getting trapped in long-term contracts.

The funding round was led by DCVC and Wing Venture Capital. It also saw participation from existing backers, including Electric Capital and Alt Capital.

In a LinkedIn post Ali Tamaseb, general partner at DCVC, said "SF Compute is building a true marketplace for compute – allowing companies to buy GPU/compute capacity on flexible, short-term contracts while enabling data centers and enterprises to sell excess capacity. This unlocks liquidity, efficiency, and price discovery in a market that has historically been rigid and hard to access."

...

Anderson. Eric Menees, Eric Park, and the rest of the team, and to be co-leading this round with Peter Wagner at Wing Venture Capital."

While SF does not own any of the GPUs it provides access to, the startup says it manages more than $100 million in hardware.

Founded in 2023, the company recently hired Eric Park, former CEO of AI cloud provider Voltage Park, as CTO. It has also hired executives from Sun Microsystems and Lambda. In total, the company now employs around 30 people.

The platform currently lists pricing information for the Nvidia H100 and H200 GPUs, though the website has a notice suggesting it will soon be offering access to B300s.

results.title: Evan Conrad Is Teaching Supercomputers How to Have an Exit | YesPress
results.author: YesPress Editorial
highlights:
A year-long GPU lease nearly emptied a two-person startup's bank account. Evan Conrad turned the mistake into SF Compute - an order book where AI companies can buy serious computing power and sell back the hours they no longer need.

...

The useful thing about a ruinous invoice is that it tends to explain itself. In 2023, Evan Conrad and Alex Gajewski were running a two-person AI audio project. To train their model, they signed for a GPU cluster for a year. The model needed about a month. The contract, having no interest in product schedules, continued for eleven more.

Their bank balance was headed toward zero. So the founders did what software people do when a system refuses to fit the problem: they made a layer around it. They found other companies that needed bursts of compute and subleased the idle months. A private rescue acquired the shape of public infrastructure. The audio project receded, and San Francisco Compute Company appeared.

Conrad now describes the company in a sentence sturdy enough to survive contact with an accountant: it sells time on large GPU clusters on contracts customers can exit. SF Compute operates the machines, offers virtual machines and bare metal, and keeps an order book where unused capacity can be listed for somebody else to buy. The escape hatch is the product.

2023 Company founded from an overlong GPU lease $40M Series A announced in late 2025 1 hr Shortest public purchasing window

...

Cloud computing trained a generation of developers to expect a tap. Open it, run a server, close it, pay for what passed through. Large GPU clusters obey a different economy. They are costly to buy, slow to build and attractive to lenders only when somebody has promised to keep paying. That promise is called offtake - the long-term purchase agreement that helps finance the cluster before it exists.

The agreement gives the builder certainty. It gives the customer a liability. An AI startup may charge its own customers month by month while owing a data center for years. If demand moves, a software roadmap can be rewritten over lunch. A warehouse of accelerators cannot pivot. Conrad's fascination sits in that mismatch between elastic ambition and stubborn assets.

...

His proposed fix is neither to abolish the long contract nor pretend the hardware is cheap. It is to make the commitment transferable. A company can reserve enough machines to get a better rate, use what it needs and list idle time on the SF Compute market. Another buyer gets a shorter window. The original buyer recovers part of the cost. SF Compute takes a fee and remains responsible for operating the cluster.

### The contract gets an escape hatch

Reserve An AI team commits to GPU capacity. → Plans move Some reserved hours become idle. → Resell Another buyer takes the listed capacity.

This is a financial idea wearing a cloud provider's overalls. It requires billing, compliance and a ledger alongside Kubernetes, InfiniBand and people who know what to do when hundreds of expensive computers disagree before breakfast. The order book matters only if the underlying hour is dependable enough to trade.

...

Traditional lease

Low

...

Conceptual comparison, not a performance measurement. Transferability creates an exit route; it does not guarantee a buyer or a resale price.

...

SF Compute's path has required its own commitments. The company says it builds data centers and the clusters inside them, supports virtual machines, bare metal, managed Slurm and Kubernetes, and can arrange contracts from one node for an hour to thousands of nodes for years. In late 2025 it raised a $40 million Series A co-led by DCVC and Wing Venture Capital. Public reports put total funding at $52 million.

results.title: "Buy everything the model touches": SF Compute CEO Evan Conrad on the reality of the compute resource market｜SecondWave｜米国株・テックトレンド
results.author: SecondWave｜米国株・テックトレンド
highlights:
Evan Conrad, CEO of the San Francisco Compute Company, appeared on a podcast to discuss the reality of the compute resource market from his perspective as a provider of GPU cluster sales and subleasing services.

...

He explains that the company is now a supercomputing firm that builds its own data centers, installs GPU clusters there, and sells them to customers in the form of contracts or leases. What makes it unique is the construction of an "order book" that allows for buying and selling between customers. When many companies purchase GPU capacity through long-term contracts of 3 to 5 years, it is a massive bet on the future, and if their reading is wrong, they risk the company itself failing. The company's goal is to allow customers to avoid such extreme risks by purchasing through SF Compute, preventing them from falling into the same plight as Stability AI. Conrad points out that this was a problem his company faced when it was just a small two-person AI lab, and it was also a problem faced by xAI. xAI was able to avoid this issue because they owned their GPU clusters, but many cloud providers do not contractually allow subleasing by customers, or even if they do, they only permit short-term subleasing for about the next hour.

...

As background, he explains that one of the reasons many companies want to purchase compute resources themselves is the concern over "residual value risk" associated with lease contracts. If a company purchases a GPU cluster but doesn't actually need that much, it would be ideal if they could at least resell the cluster to another company, but there is a structural problem in the current market where that is difficult. He also pointed out that from the perspective of a GPU cloud provider, allowing subleasing between customers would reduce their own revenue, creating a conflict of interest where it is more profitable to leave this problem unaddressed.

...

## 3. Will the price of compute resources increase tenfold?

When asked by the interviewer about prominent investor Daresh's claim that "as the value of AI increases, the price of compute resources could increase tenfold," Conrad agreed with the price increase itself but explained that complex dynamics are at play. Currently, data center capacity available for purchase in bulk is almost sold out, and building new capacity physically takes time. On the other hand, if one tries to raise the price of output (tokens), they hit the wall of the customer's budget constraints. In fact, there are customers spending on the scale of $1 billion annually on token purchases, and such customers are already under intense cost-cutting pressure to "get by with $900 million." Conrad expressed the outlook that cost pressure from these customers will lead to price-cutting efforts by major labs first, and only when that reaches its limit will the price increase of compute resources themselves truly begin in earnest.

...

Conrad repeatedly emphasized that in a world where every major company is trying to become a frontier lab, the biggest challenge is "risk." ... is not ... for ... typical large company to build ... operate ... massive supercomputer ... for ... utilization ... and existing GPU ... providers ... the ... actively ... this ... because their own revenue would decrease ... they allowed customers ... sublease to each ... He explained that SF Compute provides a mechanism to transfer that risk even when purchasing large-scale clusters as a solution to this structural problem.

results.title: Three years ago, a young founder signed a $1 million contract for GPUs. His startup needed them for 30 days. The contract ran for a year. | Pancrazio Auteri
results.author: Pancrazio Auteri
highlights: Three years ago, a young founder signed a $1 million contract for GPUs. His startup needed them for 30 days. The contract ran for a year. Evan Conrad was building an audio AI company. Like everyone, he needed compute. Like everyone, he could only get it by committing to far more than he needed. So he did something unusual: he started subleasing the idle time to other startups. The side hustle worked better than the startup. Today he runs San Francisco Compute Company, a marketplace for GPU time. That accident gave him a rare view into how the AI buildout is actually financed. In a recent Village Global interview, he explains it. It changed how I think about the whole stack. Start with the word he calls "the most important word in all of AI": offtake. Offtake is a long-term contract to buy compute BEFORE it physically exists. Think of selling apartments before building them, to convince a bank to finance the project. It is the load-bearing beam of the entire AI infra buildout. Contract first, then construction, then the bank loan. Data centers that skip this step and build on speculation get crushed. In the last downcycle, they were dumping H100 GPU time at just forty cents an hour. The next wave learned the lesson. Hence offtake contracts. So who signs these contracts? AI startups. Many of them pre-revenue. Here is the uncomfortable part. A lab raises a huge round, prepays years of compute, and burns through the deposit before it ships a product. If it fails, the first money destroyed is not the data center's loan. It is the startup's deposit, and behind it, its investors' equity. Read that again. The buildout can be sound while the valuations are inflated. Both at once. As Conrad puts it: if it exists, the AI bubble lives in the buyers' equity (the startups), not in the GPU clouds' books. There is a second lesson hiding in his business model. Selling compute looks like tech, but it does not behave like tech. A traditional SaaS company sells the same code a thousand times. It runs on cheap CPUs, so serving one more customer costs almost nothing. Generating a single video or a slide deck costs a lot of tokens, and that eats up the margins of serving a customer request. A GPU cloud pays for chips and power on every dollar it earns. Conrad's comparison is blunt: a GPU cloud is like a property manager. Marriott RUNS hotels; pension funds OWN them. That is why he thinks clusters belong with patient institutional money, and venture capital belongs elsewhere. It took one founder, stuck with eleven months of GPUs he did not need, to see how this whole industry really works. So next time you read about a trillion-dollar buildout, skip the headline number and ask the quieter question: who holds the contract when the customer's funding runs out? #AI #Infrastructure

results.title: HPC/ GPU Cluster Architect · $220k–$300k at SF Compute
highlights:
We're building the company which will de-risk the largest infrastructure build-out in history.

When people finance GPU clusters, the datacenters housing them, and the infrastructure powering them, they need "offtake" - meaning someone has signed a contract to lease the cluster for a period of time before its even built.

Financing a GPU cluster is inherently risky, since margins are thin and volumes are huge. Lenders don't want to take on the risk that cluster developers can't repay their loan, and cluster developers really don't want to risk not selling their cluster. As a result, risk is offloaded to the customer using fixed-price long-term contracts.

If you don't mitigate this customer risk, there's a bubble. This isn't SaaS anymore - application layer companies sign multi-year contracts for computer and inference, but sell to customers on monthly subscriptions. If you mess up a purchase, it's game over: a minor shift in your revenue growth rate might mean the difference between profit or bankruptcy. But what if companies could exit their contract by selling it back to the market?

Otherwise, as AI scales, compute only becomes available to folks who can effectively take on that risk. A 2-person startup in a San Francisco Victorian can't realistically sign a 5-year take or pay contract on $100m supercomputers. But they may be able to buy the month of liquidity that someone else sold back.

So that's what we make: a liquid market for GPU offtake.

results.title: AI: The AI Compute Crunch at Ground Level (part 3). AI-RTZ #1178
results.author: Michael Parekh
highlights:
The short version: prices for AI training and inference compute are being bid UP in the near term, with the squeeze falling hardest on young AI startups, while big tech incumbents and the neoclouds selling capacity are cashing in. And of course Nvidia as well, whose chips from 2022 and later are seeing rental price bumps at the cloud and neocloud companies.

...

Evan Morikawa of robotics AI startup Generalist canvassed some 17 AI cloud providers for compute this year. Last winter, providers were offering reasonable prices on contracts as short as one year. By May and June, prices had jumped, contract terms had stretched to 3 to 5 years, and clusters of the latest chips carried 12 to 18 month waits. “It’s like VC currency right now to know the current price of GPUs,” he told The Information. And: “Now 1-year contracts are almost impossible to get.”

...

A mid-size AI safety research organization talked to over 20 providers between March and July in search of just 60 chips. Three separate times, capacity that providers were advertising was sold to someone else within two days of the meeting. The org finally signed a deal worth several million dollars with Prime Intellect, reselling compute from data centers in India.

...

And at the bigger end of the neolab spectrum, Nvidia-backed Reflection AI is renting chips from SpaceXAI for $150 million a month, plus a multiyear Nebius deal totaling over $1 billion. That is a hefty chunk of the $2.5 billion the startup raised in its last round. Compute is the main use of new funds for these companies.

The number that matters most: the hourly rental price of an Nvidia H100 on a 1-year contract rose 50% from $1.73 in mid-December to $2.60 in mid-June, per Semianalysis. The H100 is a 2022 chip, TWO generations behind Nvidia’s latest. For on-demand H100s, Semianalysis often cannot quote a price at all in recent months. The column just reads ‘sold out’. 

Even at the largest cloud vendors like Amazon AWS. 

That datapoint cuts directly against the bear case argued by market shorts like Michael Burry, that AI GPUs are short-lived assets whose useful lives are overstated on the accounting books. The third-party market is voting the other way right now: four-year-old silicon is repricing UP, not down, as global demand for training and inference collide. To be fair to the bears, that is a shortage market talking, not a permanent re-rating. But the current trend lines are what they are. For the chip and cloud/neocloud vendors like CoreWeave in particular.

The sellers of AI Compute are cashing in. The Information’s Briefing by Martin Peers tells that side in “Nebius, CoreWeave Are Cashing In on Soaring AI Compute Prices”, on the heels of both neocloud earnings calls this week.

...

Pricing and margins for its newest Blackwell and Vera Rubin chips are 

> “setting new highs, while pricing for prior-generation [chips] is at or above where it was years ago.” CoreWeave raised prices 25% in July, per CFO Nitin Agrawal: “We are more confident than ever in the long-term ROI of our product.”

...

Even SpaceXAI, which pioneered the short-term premium rentals to Anthropic and Google I covered in part 1, jumped 9.7% Wednesday to $146.15, up 35% from last week. BNP Paribas notes Nebius’s short-term pricing is roughly equivalent to the economics of SpaceXAI’s recent deals. All of it under the wing of Kingmaker Nvidia, now ‘Uber AI Investor & Banker’ (AI-RTZ #1171).

...

The collision between global training and inference demand is pushing AI Compute pricing UP in the short term, even for older chips in third-party markets, with the pain concentrated on the youngest AI startups and the pricing power concentrated in the neoclouds and their Kingmaker. Consumers are paying their own version of this bill via ‘RAMageddon’ (Google just added $100 to every Pixel 11). A few years out, as those hundreds of billions of data center buildout land as live capacity, I expect the pressure to temper.

results.title: Every lender we've spoken to this year underwrites GPU fleets the same way, because it's the only way available to them. The constraint is residual value of the GPU, so naturally the … | Ronit Jain
results.author: Ronit Jain
highlights:
Every lender we've spoken to this year underwrites GPU fleets the same way, because it's the only way available to them. The constraint is residual value of the GPU, so naturally the requirement becomes multi-year contracted offtake. At Liquid Compute, we're building the instrument that makes that exposure underwritable.

...

**Reshared from Liquid Compute:**
> Mid-market compute operators have a financing problem.
>
> After several months of lender conversations, the blocker is always the same: residual value. Lenders financing a GPU fleet must believe the hardware is still worth something in year three, and this market isn't mature enough for anyone to prove that. There's no repossession history, no resale comps. A new model release can strand a previous generation of chips. As a result, lenders solve this by requiring three years of contracted offtake and size the loan against that.
>
> That protection costs the operator real money, because compute prices invert with tenor. In our own book, the same B200 capacity is $6.80 an hour month-to-month and $4.40 on a 36-month commitment. Every year of extra commitment a lender demands is revenue the operator hands to the customer, permanently, to solve someone else's risk problem.
>
> There is a way to give the lender what they're actually after without locking the operator into three years of below-market pricing:
>
> Sign 18 months of offtake rather than three years, at the materially higher rate that shorter tenor commands. Then buy a put covering the back half of that window, setting a hard floor under the price of compute.
>
> The operator books more revenue across the same fleet. Lenders can start underwriting based on a traded floor with a price on it. Residual value goes from something nobody can evidence to something the market quotes.
>
> Liquid Compute is actively working through structures like this with lenders, buyers, sellers, and operators.

results.title: There's an argument floating around that compute might get ~10x more expensive, not cheaper. The math: if a human-level software engineer can run on one H100, then at market SWE rates that … | Casey Woo
results.author: Casey Woo
highlights:
There's an argument floating around that compute might get ~10x more expensive, not cheaper. The math: if a human-level software engineer can run on one H100, then at market SWE rates that H100 should rent for over $250,000/yr. That's roughly 15x today's spot price.

Prices are already climbing. Spot is up 40%+ from the February trough, and Google reportedly pays ~$900M/month for 110K GPUs, roughly 2x spot. Lab revenue is growing ~10x a year while lab compute grows ~3x. Price closes the gap.

I have no idea if compute actually gets 10x more expensive. Forecasting the cost of anything 3 years out is a great way to be really wrong in public. But there's a line in basically every operating model I see that assumes AI gets cheaper every year. Nobody typed it in on purpose, it's just been true since 2023, and now gross margins are sitting on top of it.

results.title: 「モデルが触れるものは全部買え」SF Compute CEO Evan Conrad氏が語る計算資源市場の実像｜SecondWave｜米国株・テックトレンド
results.author: SecondWave｜米国株・テックトレンド
highlights:
現在の同社は、データセンターを自ら建設し、そこにGPUクラスターを設置したうえで、契約やリースの形で顧客に販売するスーパーコンピューティング企業だと説明する。特徴的なのは、ある顧客から別の顧客へと売買できる「オーダーブック」を構築している点だ。多くの企業が3〜5年といった長期契約でGPU容量を購入する際、それは将来に対する大きな賭けであり、もし読みが外れれば会社自体が立ち行かなくなるリスクを負う。SF Computeを介して購入すれば、そうした極端なリスクを回避でき、Stability AIのような苦境に陥らずに済むというのが同社の狙いだという。Conrad氏は、これはかつて2人だけの小さなAIラボだった自社が直面した問題であると同時に、XAIが直面した問題でもあったと指摘する。XAIはGPUクラスターを自社所有していたためにこの問題を回避できたが、多くのクラウド事業者はそもそも顧客によるサブリースを契約上認めていない、あるいは認めていても翌時間分程度の短期サブリースしか許していないという。

...

## 3. 計算資源の価格は10倍になるのか

---

対談相手が、著名投資家Daresh氏の「AIの価値が高まるにつれ、計算資源の価格は10倍になりうる」という主張について問うと、Conrad氏は、価格上昇自体には同意しつつ、複雑な力学が働くと説明した。現在、まとまった規模で購入可能なデータセンター容量はほぼ売り尽くされており、新規容量の構築には物理的に時間を要する。一方で、出力(トークン)の価格を引き上げようとすれば、顧客側の予算制約という壁にぶつかる。実際、年間10億ドル規模をトークン購入に費やしている顧客も存在し、そうした顧客はすでに「9億ドルで済ませたい」という切実なコスト削減圧力にさらされているという。Conrad氏は、まずはこうした顧客からのコスト圧力によって大手ラボ側の値下げ努力が先行し、その限界に達したところで初めて計算資源自体の価格上昇が本格化するだろうとの見通しを示した。

...

Conrad氏は、あらゆる主要企業がフロンティアラボ化しようとする世界において、最大の課題は、「リスク」だと繰り返し強調した。一般的な大企業がAI活用のために巨大なスーパーコンピューターを自ら構築・運用することは現実的ではなく、かといって既存のGPUクラウド事業者は、顧客同士のサブリースを認めてしまうと自社の収益が減るため、この問題を積極的に解決しようとするインセンティブを持たない。SF Computeはこの構造的な問題への解として、大規模なクラスターを購入しても、そのリスクを転嫁できる仕組みを提供しているのだと説明した。
